title: Contributing
text:
Thank you for your interest in improving this project. This project is open-source under the MIT license and welcomes contributions in the form of bug reports, feature requests, and pull requests.
Here is a list of important resources for contributors:

Source Code
Documentation
Issue Tracker


How to report a bug
Report bugs on the Issue Tracker.
When filing an issue, make sure to answer these questions:

Which operating system and Python version are you using?
Which version of this project are you using?
What did you do?
What did you expect to see?
What did you see instead?

The best way to get your bug fixed is to provide a test case, and/or steps to reproduce the issue.


How to request a feature
Request features on the Issue Tracker.


How to set up your development environment
You need Python and the following tools:

uv
Nox
Make
Quarto

Install the package with the existing development requirements:
$ uv sync --frozen
To also update packages, do not use the --frozen flag.
To build the documentation locally, you will also need Make and Quarto (these are non-Python dependencies).
The documentation is built with Great Docs. Its configuration is in great-docs.yml, the pages are in docs/user_guide/, and the site’s theme is in docs/theme/indigo.css. You can build the docs locally with make, which runs uv run great-docs build and writes the website to great-docs/_site/. Run make preview to serve it locally.
The timings table on the features page is built from benchmarks/results.csv. To update it, run uv run python benchmarks/benchmark.py from the repository root and commit the updated file. Each run is appended to that file along with the date, the package and pyfixest versions and a description of the machine, so it also serves as a performance log. The docs show the most recent run.
To publish new docs to GitHub Pages (where the documentation is displayed as web pages), it’s make publish—but only devs with admin rights will be able to execute this.


How to test the project
Run the full test suite:
$ uv run nox
List the available Nox sessions:
$ uv run nox --list-sessions
You can also run a specific Nox session. For example, invoke the unit test suite like this:
$ uv run nox --session=tests
Unit tests are located in the tests directory, and are written using the pytest testing framework.
You may need to use, for example, uv run nox to ensure that the tests are run in the right environment.
For the pre-commit checks, use
$ uv run pre-commit run --all-files


How to submit changes
Open a pull request to submit changes to this project.
Your pull request needs to meet the following guidelines for acceptance:

The Nox test suite must pass without errors and warnings.
Include unit tests. This project aims to maintain 98% code coverage.
If your changes add functionality, update the documentation accordingly.
Run make to generate the new documentation.
Run the pre-commit suite before committing.

Feel free to submit early, though—we can always iterate on this.
To run linting and code formatting checks before committing your change, you need to run the following command:
$ uv run nox --session=pre-commit -- install
It is recommended to open an issue before starting work on anything. This will allow a chance to talk it over with the owners and validate your approach.


How to create a package release

Open a new branch with the version name
Change the version in pyproject.toml using uv version --bump <major|minor|patch>
Commit the change with a new version label as the commit message (checking the tests pass)
Head to GitHub and merge into main (again, if the CI works)
The release GitHub Action then sees that the version has changed. It tags the merge commit with the new version, publishes the package to PyPI, publishes the release notes that Release Drafter has been collecting from merged pull requests, and publishes the documentation. Don’t create the tag yourself: if the tag already exists, the action treats the push as an ordinary one.

Every other push to main publishes a developmental release (the next patch version with a .dev<timestamp> suffix) to TestPyPI and checks that the documentation builds.
If you ever need distributable files, you can use the uv build command locally.


How to build the documentation manually and locally
You shouldn’t need to publish the documentation because there’s a GitHub action that covers it automatically whenever there’s a new release. But to upload the documentation manually, it’s

Run make to build the documentation
Run make publish to publish the documentation

# Specification Curve

Specification curve analysis for econometrics, built on pyfixest

## Installation

```bash
pip install specification_curve
```

## API overview

### Classes

The main entry point. Describe the specifications, estimate them, and plot the curve.

- `SpecificationCurve`: Runs and plots every variant of a regression specification

### Functions

Plot a results table directly, and select subsets of specifications.

- `plot_curve`: Draws a specification curve
- `subsets_by`: Builds a ``subsets`` argument with one sample per level of a column

### Example data

Data sets used in the documentation and tests.

- `load_example_panel`: Generates a synthetic firm-year panel
- `load_example_data1`: Retrieves example data from a file included with the package
- `load_example_data2`: Generates example data with one outcome and four regressors
- `load_example_data3`: Generates example data with two outcomes, where the true effect of x1 is 0.4

## Resources

- [Full documentation](https://aeturrell.github.io/specification_curve/)
- [llms.txt](llms.txt) — Indexed API reference for LLMs
- [llms-full.txt](llms-full.txt) — Comprehensive documentation for LLMs

title: plot_curve()
text:
Draws a specification curve.


Usage
Source


plot_curve(
    results,
    null_curves=None,
    *,
    alpha=0.05,
    ci_levels=None,
    sort_by="estimate",
    color_by="significance",
    panels=None,
    labels=None,
    highlight=None,
    show_median=True,
    show_nobs=False,
    colors=None,
    figsize=None,
    fig=None,
    style=True
)


The top panel shows the focal estimate of every specification with its confidence interval(s). Below it, one panel per dimension that varies shows which choice each specification makes. Specifications that could not be estimated are left out.
The function works on any data frame with the columns of SpecificationCurve.results, so results that were saved, filtered or combined from several curves can be drawn too. It does not call plt.show() and does not change matplotlib’s global settings.


Parameters


results: pd.DataFrame

Results as produced by SpecificationCurve.fit.

null_curves: Optional[pd.DataFrame] = None

Quantiles of the curve under the null, as produced by SpecificationCurve.fit_null. Can only be shown when sorting by estimate.

alpha: float = 0.05

Significance level used when colouring by significance.

ci_levels: Optional[Sequence[float]] = None

Which of the stored confidence levels to draw. By default, all of them.

sort_by: Union[str, Sequence[str]] = "estimate"

Order of the specifications: “estimate”, another column of the results, or a list of columns. Ties are ordered by estimate.

color_by: str = "significance"

“significance” colours estimates by sign and significance. A dimension (“y”, “x”, “fe”, “iv”, “vcov”, “model”, “weights” or “subset”) colours by the value of that dimension and adds a legend.

panels: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None

Which dimensions to show under the curve, in order. By default, every dimension that varies.

labels: Optional[Mapping[str, str]] = None

Replacement display text for panel titles (keyed by dimension, e.g. {"fe": "Fixed effects"}) and for values (keyed by the value, e.g. {"firm + year": "Firm and year"}).

highlight: Union[Selector, Sequence[Selector], None] = None

A preferred specification to mark and annotate, given as a spec_id, a dict of column values (e.g. {"y": "log(wage)", "controls": ["age"], "fe": None}) or a query string. It must match exactly one specification. Pass a list to mark several.

show_median: bool = True

Draw a line at the median estimate.

show_nobs: bool = False

Add a panel with the number of observations used by each specification.

colors: ColorSpec = None

Colours to use. When colouring by significance, a dict with any of the keys “positive”, “negative”, “insignificant”. When colouring by a dimension, a list of colours or a dict keyed by the dimension’s values.

figsize: Optional[tuple[float, float]] = None

Figure size in inches. By default, chosen from the number of panels.

fig: Union[Figure, SubFigure, None] = None

An existing figure or subfigure to draw into. By default a new figure is created.

style: bool = True

Use this package’s fonts and sizes for the figure.





Returns


 tuple[Union[Figure, SubFigure], dict[str, Axes]]

tuple[Union[Figure, SubFigure], dict[str, Axes]]: The figure and its axes keyed by panel name: “curve”, then the dimensions shown, then “nobs” if requested.





Raises


 ValueError

If no specification was estimated successfully, or an argument does not fit the results.

title: SpecificationCurve
text:
fit()

Estimates the specifications.


Usage
Source


fit(
    *,
    ci_levels=(0.95,),
    n_jobs=1,
    max_specs=None,
    seed=None,
    on_error="record",
    keep_models=False,
    batch=True,
    progress=None,
    **kwargs
)


Parameters


ci_levels: Sequence[float] = (0.95,)

Confidence levels to store. Each gives a pair of columns such as ci_low_95 and ci_high_95.

n_jobs: int = 1

Number of parallel workers.

max_specs: Optional[int] = None

Estimate a random sample of this many specifications instead of the whole grid.

seed: Optional[int] = None

Seed for the random sample.

on_error: str = "record"

“record” keeps specifications that fail in the results with their error message; “raise” stops at the first failure.

keep_models: bool = False

Keep the fitted pyfixest models in .models, keyed by spec_id. Specifications that differ only in vcov share one model object.

batch: bool = True

Send specifications that share a sample, estimator, focal regressor and fixed effects to pyfixest in a single call. The results are the same either way.

progress: Optional[bool] = None

Show a progress bar. By default one is shown when there are many pyfixest calls to make.

**kwargs: Any

Passed to the pyfixest estimators, for example ssc, fixef_rm, demeaner or context. Each estimator receives the arguments it accepts.





Returns


SpecificationCurve: SpecificationCurve

The object itself, so calls can be chained.





Raises


 TypeError

If a keyword argument is not accepted by any of the estimators in the grid.

title: SpecificationCurve
text:
fit_null()

Tests the curve against the null hypothesis of no effect.


Usage
Source


fit_null(
    n_boot=500,
    *,
    method="auto",
    cluster=None,
    strata=None,
    alpha=0.05,
    alternative="two-sided",
    seed=None,
    n_jobs=1,
    keep_draws=False,
    min_valid=0.5,
    progress=None
)


The curve is re-estimated on many resamples in which the null holds. Three statistics of the observed curve are then compared with their distribution across resamples: the median estimate, the share of significant estimates, and Stouffer’s Z, which combines the evidence of all specifications. The results are in .null_summary and .null_curves.
With method="bootstrap", each specification’s estimated effect is removed from its outcome and rows are resampled with replacement. This applies when every specification uses model="feols". method="bayesian-bootstrap" (the Bayesian bootstrap of Rubin, 1981; see Andrews, Moon and Shapiro, 2026) imposes the null in the same way and has the same requirement, but gives rows random Dirichlet weights instead of resampling them, so that no row (or cluster) is ever left out. With method="permutation", the focal variable is shuffled between rows. This applies to any estimator, but it is only valid if the focal variable is as good as randomly assigned (within strata, if given), as in an experiment, and it does not apply to instrumental-variable specifications.


Parameters


n_boot: int = 500

Number of resamples. Use several hundred for results you rely on; every resample re-estimates the whole curve.

method: str = "auto"

“bootstrap”, “bayesian-bootstrap”, “permutation” or “auto”. “auto” uses the bootstrap if every specification uses “feols”, and otherwise asks you to choose.

cluster: Optional[str] = None

Column identifying clusters. Whole clusters are resampled (bootstrap), share one weight (Bayesian bootstrap) or swap their focal values (permutation; the focal variable must be constant within them).

strata: Optional[str] = None

Column identifying strata. Resampling is done within each stratum.

alpha: float = 0.05

Significance level for the share of significant estimates.

alternative: str = "two-sided"

“two-sided”, “greater” (the effect is positive) or “less” (the effect is negative).

seed: Optional[int] = None

Seed for the resampling. Results do not depend on n_jobs.

n_jobs: int = 1

Number of parallel workers.

keep_draws: bool = False

Keep the estimates from every resample in .null_draws.

min_valid: float = 0.5

A resample is left out if fewer than this share of the specifications could be estimated in it.

progress: Optional[bool] = None

Show a progress bar. By default one is shown when there are at least 20 resamples.





Returns


SpecificationCurve: SpecificationCurve

The object itself, so calls can be chained.

title: Specification Curve
text:
Specification curve analysis for Python
    Specification Curve
    Run every defensible regression and see all of the estimates in one chart.
    uv add specification-curve
    
      See the features
      API reference
    
  
  
    
    Replay
  


Specification Curve is a Python package that performs specification curve analysis; it helps with the problem of the “garden of forking paths” (many defensible choices) when doing analysis by running many regressions and summarising the effects in an easy to digest chart. Estimation is done by pyfixest, so specifications can vary the outcome, the regressor of interest, controls, fixed effects, instruments, standard errors, weights, the sample and the estimator (OLS, Poisson, logit, probit and quantile regression).

      


Introduction
When specifying a causal model, modellers have a number of options. These can be informed by field intelligence, priors, and even misguided attempts to find a significant result. Even with the best of intentions, research teams can reach entirely different conclusions using the same, or similar, data because of different choices made in preparing data or in modelling it.
Typically this happens when there isn’t a clear way to do “feature engineering” on the data or the data are imperfect in some way. For example, you have a high frequency time series which needs to be aggregated to a lower frequency: you could take the maximum, the minimum, or the average over each high frequency time period. A different choice may be appropriate in different settings.
There’s formal evidence that researchers really do make different decisions; one study (Silberzahn et al. 2018) gave the same research question—whether soccer referees are more likely to give red cards to players with dark skin tones than to players with light skin tones—to 29 different teams. From the abstract of that paper:

Analytic approaches varied widely across the teams, and the estimated effect sizes ranged from 0.89 to 2.93 (Mdn = 1.31) in odds-ratio units. Twenty teams (69%) found a statistically significant positive effect, and 9 teams (31%) did not observe a significant relationship. Overall, the 29 different analyses used 21 unique combinations of covariates. Neither analysts’ prior beliefs about the effect of interest nor their level of expertise readily explained the variation in the outcomes of the analyses. Peer ratings of the quality of the analyses also did not account for the variability.

So not only can different decisions made, but there seems to be no clearly identifiable reason for them!
There have since been a number of papers that find similar conclusions (Huntington-Klein et al. 2021).
Specification curves have been invented (Simonsohn et al. 2020) as a way to better grasp the garden of forking paths that analysts face, and help them show how sensitive their results are to alternative specifications.
More than one piece of software (Masur and Scharkow 2019) has appeared to help researchers and analysts use this technique: specification curve is one such package!


Quickstart
Here’s an example of using Specification Curve. The example data are a made-up panel of firms, in which being treated raises log sales by 0.3, but firms that would have had high sales anyway are more likely to be treated.
We ask how the estimated effect of treatment depends on which controls are included, whether firm and year fixed effects are used, and how the standard errors are computed.

sco = sc.SpecificationCurve(
    df,
    y="log(sales)",
    x="treated",
    controls=["size", "leverage", "rd"],
    fe=[None, "firm", "firm + year"],
    vcov=["hetero", {"CRV1": "firm"}],
)
sco.fit()
sco.plot();








Each column is one specification. The top panel shows the estimated coefficient on treated with its confidence interval, and the panels underneath show which choices that specification makes. Markers are coloured blue when the coefficient is positive and significant (at the 0.05 level), red when it is negative and significant, and black otherwise.
Here, the specifications without firm fixed effects overstate the effect, and those with them are close to the true value.
You can also describe the specifications with a pyfixest formula. Its multiple-estimation operators define the choices: several outcomes (y1 + y2 ~ ...), sw() (one of these terms at a time) and sw0() (one at a time, or none). Specification Curve adds comb() and comb0(), which stand for every combination of their terms (with comb0() including none of them). The x argument names the coefficient to plot.
This formula describes the same specifications as above:

sco = sc.SpecificationCurve(
    df,
    "log(sales) ~ treated + comb0(size, leverage, rd) | sw0(firm, firm + year)",
    x="treated",
    vcov=["hetero", {"CRV1": "firm"}],
)
sco.fit()
sco.plot();








The features page shows everything else: other estimators, instrumental variables, samples, customising the chart, and statistical inference on the curve as a whole.


Installation
You can install Specification Curve via uv:
$ uv add specification-curve
To install the development version from git, use:
$ pip install git+https://github.com/aeturrell/specification_curve.git


License
Distributed under the terms of the MIT license.


Citing Specification Curve
You can find full citation information at the following link: https://zenodo.org/badge/latestdoi/282989537.
Using Specification Curve in your paper? Let us know by raising an issue beginning with “citation”.


Similar Packages
In RStats, there is specr (which inspired many design choices in this package) and spec_chart. Some of the example data in this package is the same as in specr, but please note that results have not been cross-checked across packages.


References


Huntington-Klein, Nick, Andreu Arenas, Emily Beam, et al. 2021. “The Influence of Hidden Researcher Decisions in Applied Microeconomics.” Economic Inquiry 59 (3): 944–60.


Masur, Philipp K., and Michael Scharkow. 2019. Specr: Statistical Functions for Conducting Specification Curve Analyses (Version 0.2.1). https://github.com/masurp/specr.


Silberzahn, Raphael, Eric L Uhlmann, Daniel P Martin, et al. 2018. “Many Analysts, One Data Set: Making Transparent How Variations in Analytic Choices Affect Results.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 1 (3): 337–56.

title: Features
text: Let’s see Specification Curve’s features in action.

title: Features
text:
Missing values
In the example data, age and leverage have some missing values. (Firm age rises by one each year, so it should not be combined with firm and year fixed effects together: pyfixest would drop it as collinear.) By default, within each sample every specification is estimated on the same rows: those that are complete for all the variables used by any specification. That way differences between estimates come from the specification and not from a changing sample. Passing common_sample=False lets each specification use every row it can instead. The number of observations each one used is in the results, and show_nobs=True adds it to the chart.

sco = sc.SpecificationCurve(
    df,
    y="log(sales)",
    x="treated",
    controls=["size", "age", "leverage"],
    common_sample=False,
)
sco.fit()
sco.plot(show_nobs=True);

title: Features
text:
Choosing a resampling method
There are three ways of generating data in which the null is true, chosen with method:

"bootstrap" (the default for linear models). Each specification’s estimated effect is removed from its outcome, y^* = y - \hat\beta x, so that the regressor of interest has no effect on y^* by construction, and then rows (or whole clusters) are drawn with replacement.
"bayesian-bootstrap", the Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin 1981; Andrews et al. 2026). The null is imposed in the same way, but instead of drawing rows with replacement every row (or cluster) is kept and given a random weight from a flat Dirichlet distribution, scaled so that the weights average one. Where the ordinary bootstrap gives each row a whole number of copies, possibly zero, the Bayesian bootstrap gives it a positive, continuously varying weight.
"permutation". The regressor of interest is shuffled between rows (or clusters), which breaks any link between it and the outcome.

Which methods you can use depends on the estimators and designs in the curve:

† Only valid if the regressor of interest is as good as randomly assigned (within strata, if given). ‡ The random weights multiply your own; your weights must be analytic weights (pyfixest’s default, weights_type="aweights").
The two bootstraps need every specification to be linear because removing \hat\beta x from the outcome only imposes the null in a linear model: in a Poisson model or a logit it does not. If the curve mixes linear and non-linear estimators, method="auto" raises an error and asks you to choose. Permutation is not available for instrumental-variable specifications, because shuffling the endogenous regressor but not its instruments breaks the first stage.

title: Features
text:
The Bayesian bootstrap
The two bootstraps give very similar answers in large samples. The Bayesian bootstrap does better when resampling can produce data in which a specification cannot be estimated. With the ordinary bootstrap a resample may, by chance, contain no treated units, no rows of some fixed-effect level, or too few clusters; the specifications that cannot be estimated are missing from that resample, and a resample in which fewer than min_valid of them could be estimated is left out (with a warning). Because the Bayesian bootstrap never leaves a row out, that does not happen. Its null distributions are also smoother, which helps with few clusters.
Here is an extreme case: eight clusters, only one of them treated. Every ordinary bootstrap resample that misses the treated cluster has no variation in the regressor of interest.

import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
small = pd.DataFrame({"group": np.repeat(np.arange(8), 5), "a": rng.normal(size=40)})
small["x"] = (small["group"] == 0).astype(float)
small["y"] = small["a"] + 0.5 * small["x"] + rng.normal(size=40)
sco_small = sc.SpecificationCurve(small, y="y", x="x", controls=["a"]).fit()

for method in ["bootstrap", "bayesian-bootstrap"]:
    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
        warnings.simplefilter("always")
        sco_small.fit_null(
            n_boot=200, method=method, cluster="group", seed=0, progress=False
        )
    left_out = [str(w.message) for w in caught if "left out" in str(w.message)]
    print(f"{method}: {left_out[0] if left_out else 'no resamples were left out.'}")

bootstrap: 79 of 200 resamples were left out because fewer than 50% of the specifications could be estimated in them.
bayesian-bootstrap: no resamples were left out.

    x="treated",
    controls=["size", "leverage"],
    fe=["firm", "firm + year"],
    vcov={"CRV1": "firm"},
)
sco.fit()
sco.fit_null(n_boot=50, method="bayesian-bootstrap", cluster="firm", seed=0)
sco.null_summary
